name: Amancio Ortega
title: The Billionaire Who Never Had an Office
subtitle: A railway worker's son becomes an errand boy in a shirt shop, then founds Zara and Inditex, and somehow stays almost invisible the whole way.
hook: By the late 1990s his clothes were sold around the world, yet no photograph of Amancio Ortega had ever been published. The first one appeared in Inditex's first annual report in ==1999==, a plain shot of a serious man in a white shirt and dark jacket. Before that, there were rumours that the founder of Zara **did not even exist**.

contact.howToReach: Amancio Ortega has no social media at all: his own foundation says so in writing, so any account using his name is not his. He almost never gives interviews and no channel reaches him personally, but his companies publish real doors: journalists can write to press@inditex.com, shareholders to ir@inditex.com or accionistas@inditex.com, and Zara shoppers with an order problem should use the help section on zara.com. Do not pitch a startup or ask for money: the Fundación Amancio Ortega says it does not finance private initiatives and that neither Ortega nor its chair Flora Pérez ever asks anyone for money or gives investment tips, so treat any such message as a scam. The one open application is the foundation's scholarship for a school year in the US or Canada, and it is only for students in Spain. If you do write to Inditex, send three or four sentences in English or Spanish: who you are, the one thing you want, and why it matters to their business.

chapters.title: The Boy From the Railway House

blocks.text: Amancio Ortega Gaona was born on ==28 March 1936== in Busdongo de Arbas, a mountain village in the province of León, in northern Spain. Fortune magazine described it as a hamlet of about 60 people. He was the youngest of four children in a family with very little money.

Busdongo sits more than 1,200 metres up in the mountains, on the railway line that links the dry plateau of Castile with Asturias on the coast. In winter, heavy snow could cut the village off from the world. The Ortega family lived in a railway house built right beside the tracks.

photo.caption: Busdongo station after a snowfall, 2015. A future billionaire was born in this tiny railway village in 1936.
photo.author: VivirElTren.es

blocks.text: Born beside a railway line. Watch how trains steer his whole childhood.

The railway was the family's whole world. His father, Antonio Ortega, worked for the railways, and that job decided where the family lived. Ortega told his biographer that his father, a native of Valladolid, was posted to Busdongo to look after the signal gear, checking that the points and tracks were in good order. Some Spanish reports call him the head of the little station, but his son's own account is the better source.

His mother, Josefa Gaona, kept the home running. English-language profiles say she also worked as a housemaid, cleaning other people's houses to bring in money. Spanish reports describe the household as humble.

A railway wage was small. Drawing on his biographer, the French paper Le Petit Journal reported that local shopkeepers often had to let the Ortegas buy on credit. In plain words, the family bought food now and promised to pay later, when the next wage came in.
En casa no había nada de nada, pero nos educaron con valores.
blocks.who: Recollection quoted in Covadonga O'Shea's 2008 biography Así es Amancio Ortega, as reported by El Cronista

blocks.text: Translated, that line means: at home there was nothing at all, but they raised us with values. It comes from Así es Amancio Ortega, the 2008 book by the journalist Covadonga O'Shea. Her book was built on long conversations with Ortega himself and with his relatives, friends and colleagues, which makes it the closest thing we have to his own account.
A few weeks in the snow, then the Basque Country

The family did not stay in Busdongo for long. Diario de León says they left after only a few weeks, and other reports say Amancio was still a baby. His father's railway job moved them east to Tolosa, a small industrial town in Gipuzkoa, in Spain's Basque Country.

So the first home he could actually remember was not in León at all. It was Tolosa, where he spent his early childhood. The family stayed there until the railway transferred his father again, in ==1944==.

photo.caption: Tolosa, Gipuzkoa, in 1941. Amancio was about five, living here because of his father's railway posting.
photo.author: Vicente Martín (Foto Car collection, Kutxa Fototeka)

blocks.text: He was born in 1936, the year the Spanish Civil War began. Spanish accounts of his early life place it in the hard years after that war, when ordinary families like his had very little. A boy born in that time and place had no reason to expect anything special.

For example: Amancio Ortega and the Peruvian novelist Mario Vargas Llosa were born on exactly the same day, 28 March 1936. One became one of the most famous writers in the Spanish language. The other had, by 2013, become the third-richest person in the world, according to Fortune.
A new city by the sea

In 1944 the railway moved the family once more, this time to A Coruña. It is a port city on the Atlantic coast of Galicia, in the far north-west corner of Spain. This is where Amancio grew up, and it is the city he never really left.

Count the moves. Before he was nine, Amancio had lived in three very different corners of Spain: the snowy mountains of León, the Basque Country and the Atlantic coast of Galicia. Each move happened because a railway office somewhere decided where his father was needed. The boy learned early that his family had very little control over its own life.

In A Coruña the family lived in a row house that backed onto the train tracks, a home that doubled as housing for railway workers. Galicia had few jobs, and many of its men worked at sea. Remember that detail, because it matters later in this story.
Every move so far was decided by someone else's job.
The day at the shop counter

The scene that shaped his life happened at a shop counter. One afternoon after school, Amancio went with his mother to a local grocery, where she asked, once again, to buy on credit. He says the counter was so high that he could not see who was speaking. This time the answer was no.
He heard someone say, 'Señora, I cannot give this to you. You have to pay for it.'
blocks.who: Covadonga O'Shea, his biographer, speaking to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: O'Shea told Fortune that the boy felt deeply humiliated. In the extracts her publisher released, he recalls the shopkeeper telling Señora Josefa that there could be no more credit, and then adds the two short sentences below. They mean: that left me destroyed, I was barely twelve. Fortune gives his age as 13. O'Shea's book came out in 2008, so he was in his seventies when he told her this.
Aquello me dejó destrozado. Yo tenía apenas doce años.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, in Covadonga O'Shea's Así es Amancio Ortega (2008), publisher's extract

blocks.text: What he did next is the important part. He decided to start working, earn money and help his family, and he chose never to go back to school. O'Shea sees this moment as the root of the extreme work ethic that everyone who knows him describes.
Shame became fuel. Read this twice.

It would be easy to turn this into a movie scene where a poor boy swears to become a billionaire. But that is not what the sources say. __He did not set out to get rich. He set out to make sure his family never stood at that counter again.__ The fortune came later, as a side effect of solving that much smaller, much more personal problem.
School, briefly

Very little is reliably known about his classroom years. The Spanish news site Vozpópuli reports that at about 12 he was a pupil at a Colegio del Sagrado Corazón, a Catholic school, and that he left early, reportedly to help the family's finances. He never received any higher education.

Sources disagree on his exact age when he walked out of school for good. Some say 13, others say 14. He told O'Shea himself that it is true he started work at 13. Either way, he was still a child, and he has been working ever since.

For example: if Amancio had grown up in India today, he would have left school somewhere around Class 8. No board exams, no college applications, no degree. Everything he later knew about clothes, money and people, he learned on the job.

chapters.title: The Errand Boy Who Watched Everything

blocks.text: Around the age of 13 or 14, Amancio got his first job. He became a recadero, an errand boy, at Gala, a shirt shop in A Coruña. It was the bottom rung of the clothing trade, and it was where his real education began.

Gala made shirts for wealthy customers. As the delivery boy, Amancio carried the finished clothes through the streets and ran whatever errands the shop needed. It was humble work, and he took it because the family needed the money.

Amazingly, Gala was still trading on the same downtown corner in 2013. Its owner then, José Martínez, had inherited the shop from his father. Martínez and Amancio first became friends at Gala when they were both ==14 years old==.
No one ever comes in here to buy anything. They just want to know about Amancio.
blocks.who: José Martínez, owner of the Gala shirt shop and Ortega's teenage friend, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: Fortune gives us one lovely, ordinary picture of those teenage years. The two boys spent their afternoons folding shirts at Gala and then riding their bikes around town. No grand plans, no business school, just two teenagers doing their job and then going out.

Decades later, the little shirt shop became an odd kind of landmark. Martínez told Fortune that visitors came in not to buy shirts but to ask about the errand boy who had once worked there. The most famous thing Gala ever produced, it turned out, was not a shirt at all.
He was 14 here, folding other people's shirts.
What a delivery boy can see

A delivery job sounds boring, but it gave Amancio an unusual view of the whole business. After Gala he worked as an assistant to drapers and tailors, the people who sold cloth and made clothes to measure. Moving between these jobs, he watched how a piece of clothing travelled from the designer, to the workshop, to the shop, and finally to the customer.

He noticed something that most people in the trade simply accepted. Every time a garment passed from one set of hands to the next, its cost went up. The International Directory of Business Biographies says this lesson convinced him that the way to win was to get products to customers directly, without a chain of middlemen.

For example: think of a shirt's journey as a relay race. The cloth seller adds a margin, the tailor adds a margin, the shop adds a margin, and each handover takes time. Young Amancio was the runner who saw every handover, and he realised that a business owning the whole race could be both cheaper and faster.

Fortune reports that by the age of ==16==, he had reached a clear conclusion. The real money, he believed, was in giving customers exactly what they wanted, and giving it to them quickly. To do that, he would need to control the whole supply chain himself.
Sixteen years old. This idea later powered Zara's entire model.

__Most teenagers in a job only see their own small task. Amancio studied the whole system around him.__ That habit of watching, asking why things cost what they cost, and imagining a shorter path is the single most useful thing a young worker can copy from him.
La Maja: a family shop floor

His next big step was La Maja, a clothing and haberdashery shop in A Coruña. His older brother Antonio and his sister Josefa, known as Pepita, already worked there. Accounts differ on the timing: one Spanish report says he started there as an errand boy at 14, while others place his move after his years at Gala.

He started at the bottom again and earned the owners' trust. Over time he was promoted from errand boy to dependiente, a shop assistant serving customers at the counter. For a teenager who had left school, this was a real step up.

Behind that counter he picked up what El Español calls key knowledge about the business and about how customers behave. He saw which pieces people wanted, which they could not afford, and which sat unsold on the shelves. This was market research, years before he had a word for it.

blocks.text: The girl from La Maja

La Maja is also where he met Rosalía Mera, the woman who would become his first wife and business partner. Rosalía was born in A Coruña in 1944, about eight years after Amancio. Her parents were factory workers.
Her story mirrors his. She left school at just ==11== to work as a sales assistant at La Maja. Like Amancio, she learned the clothing trade standing behind a shop counter, not sitting in a classroom.
Two kids who left school early. Together they'd build an empire.
The hunger

People who have studied his life keep coming back to one word. Xabier R. Blanco, a local journalist who co-wrote an unauthorised biography of Ortega, told Fortune that poverty had given the young man a drive that never switched off.
There was a hunger.
blocks.who: Xabier R. Blanco, co-author of an unauthorised biography of Ortega, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: Spanish reports sum up those years in one simple line: he started working at 14 and has not stopped since. Put that next to the scene at the shop counter and you understand the teenager. He was not chasing status or fun. He was making sure the family was safe.
Almost nothing reliable survives about his teenage reading. We won't make it up.

blocks.title: Your first job is a classroom
blocks.text: Amancio's first jobs paid very little, but he treated them like a free course in how his industry worked. Wherever you work at 16 or 19, a café, a shop, an internship, notice where the money goes, where time is wasted and what customers keep asking for. That notebook is your future business plan.

chapters.title: From Shop Counter to Kitchen Table

blocks.text: Amancio Ortega never went to university, and he had no formal higher education of any kind. His school was the shop floor. A Spanish profile sums up his start simply: he began in textiles at 14, working as a shop assistant in two well-known clothing stores.

Through the 1950s he kept climbing inside the trade. By the early 1960s he had become the manager of a local clothing shop. Spanish press accounts connect his rise with La Maja, the shop where his brother and sister worked.
No degree. Still running a shop in his mid-twenties.
The manager who noticed who wasn't buying
As manager, he saw a problem that sat in plain view. The garments in the shop were lovely, but only the wealthy people of the city could afford them. Everyone else looked, touched and walked away.
Very important for first-time founders! Look at who can't afford it.

So he started making cheaper versions himself. He bought less expensive fabric in Barcelona, cut the pieces by hand using patterns made of cardboard, and sold the finished clothes to local shops. It was a side project, built with his own hands and his own savings.

One product stood out: the quilted housecoat, or bata, worn at home by the well-off women of A Coruña. Working with his brother and sister, their partners and Rosalía, he made these housecoats and sold them for less than the competition. Later the family added men's shirts and sportswear.

For example: picture a smart quilted housecoat that only A Coruña's richer families could buy. The Ortegas made a similar one with cheaper cloth, hand-cut pieces and almost no overheads, then sold it below the shop price. Same look, lower price, and a whole new group of customers who could finally say yes.

This was not a factory yet. El Español reports that he and Rosalía began by making clothes from home. __The business behind thousands of stores around the world started as two shop workers making clothes at home.__
A family firm takes shape
The early business was a family affair, and everyone had a clear role. Amancio ran the design side. His brother Antonio led the commercial work of selling, and his sister Josefa kept the books.

Josefa's role was not a small one. El Español notes that she kept the company's accounts from the very beginning. In a tiny business with no investors and no safety net, the person who watches every peseta can decide whether the company lives or dies.
Design, sales, money. Every startup needs these three seats filled.

In ==1963==, at the age of 27, Amancio turned the side project into a real company: Confecciones GOA. Many profiles say the name hid a small joke: his own initials, Amancio Ortega Gaona, written backwards. A 2025 history in the Spanish paper ARA says it came from the initials of Amancio and his brother Antonio Ortega Gaona.
Amancio Ortega opens Confecciones GOA, a small dressmaking workshop.

blocks.text: The money to start came from the business itself. He used the profits from his cheaper copies to open his first factory in 1963. Forbes describes the start the same modest way: a small family company making clothes.

That matters more than it sounds. Inditex, today one of the biggest clothing companies in the world, still counts 1963 and this small workshop as its beginning. Forbes lists his fortune as self-made: there was no inheritance, no wealthy backer and no family company to take over, only the family he worked beside.

blocks.text: The women of Galicia

Remember those Galician families where the men were away at sea? Amancio turned that into his workforce. Fortune reports that he began organising thousands of local women into sewing cooperatives, small groups who made the garments while GOA handled design and sales.

One of those workers, Mercedes López, started working for him at just 14, about the age he had been at Gala. Decades later, she told Fortune that the conditions had been good and that the boss was close to the people on the sewing floor.
We knew Amancio well. He was very close to the workers.
blocks.who: Mercedes López, who began sewing for GOA at 14, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: GOA's quilted bathrobes sold well, and the little firm grew. Fortune describes a thriving production of bathrobes for this first company. The boy who once carried other people's shirts now had a team making his own designs.
Partners in work and life

Rosalía Mera was part of the business from the very start. Reports at her death in 2013 said she and Ortega began by making women's bathrobes together. In ==1966==, three years after GOA was founded, the two married.

Think about who these founders were. He was a railway worker's son who left school at 13 or 14. She had left school at 11. Neither had a degree, a rich parent or an investor, yet between them they knew more about real customers than most fashion executives of the time.
No investors. No degrees. Just skill, family and customers.
Two blocks from where it began

GOA was the seed. Twelve years later, on ==9 May 1975==, the couple opened their own shop on the ground floor of numbers 64 and 66, Juan Flórez Street, in A Coruña. It stood just two blocks from Gala, the shirt shop where Amancio had started as an errand boy.

He wanted to call it Zorba, after the film Zorba the Greek. Obituaries of Rosalía Mera reported that a bar nearby already used the name, so the letters made for the sign were reused to spell a new word. The shop became Zara.

photo.caption: The first Zara shop on Juan Flórez Street, A Coruña, photographed in 2012. It opened in 1975, two blocks from the shirt shop where Amancio began as an errand boy.
photo.author: Nemigo

blocks.text: Two blocks from where he delivered shirts as a boy. Two.

That shop is where the next part of this book begins. But almost every idea that made Zara famous was already present in these early years: watch the customer, cut out the middlemen, move fast and keep control of making the clothes. Ortega himself has always said he did not do it alone.
No he estado solo en esto y no merezco ningún reconocimiento más que el del trabajo y la fortuna de haberme rodeado de los mejores.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, quoted from Covadonga O'Shea's biography (via Europa Press)

blocks.text: In English, he is saying that he has not been alone in this, and that he deserves no credit except for the work and for the luck of surrounding himself with the best people. For him, those people started with a brother who sold, a sister who counted the money and a young woman from La Maja who sewed beside him.

blocks.title: Start with the customer who is being left out
blocks.text: Amancio's first product was not a new invention. It was a copy of something the rich already wore, made cheap enough for everyone else. Look around your own city for things people want but cannot afford, and ask what would have to change to bring the price down.

blocks.title: Fund the first step with the business itself
blocks.text: He had no investors. He made and sold a few pieces, kept the profit, and used it to build the next step. A small business that pays for itself from day one teaches you more, and owes less, than a big idea waiting for funding.

People usually describe Amancio Ortega as a man with one company. That is only half true. Behind Zara sits a workshop that made dressing gowns, a holding company that went public, eight different store chains, two chains that flopped and were shut, and a private investment firm that now owns office towers, ports and power-grid stakes on four continents.

This chapter goes through every one of them in order, the wins and the failures. For each one, look at four things: what problem it solved, why he picked it, where the first money came from, and what really happened. __The pattern is simple: every business here was started with his own money or the group's money, not investors'. Each one was paid for by the one before it.__
Watch the money: each business funds the next one.

blocks.name: Confecciones GOA
blocks.idea: In the early 1960s, a good dressing gown was an expensive thing in the shops of A Coruña, in north-west Spain. Ortega's idea was to copy a popular, pricey dressing gown, make it with cheaper materials and sell it for much less. Later reporting says one of the first hits was a bathrobe copied from a model bought in Catalonia, which sold in A Coruña shops for 140 pesetas.
blocks.decision: He had worked in clothing shops since he was a young teenager: first as a delivery boy for the Gala shirt shop, then at a shop called La Maja. By the early 1960s he was a shop manager. He could have stayed a safe employee. Instead he chose to make the product himself, and he chose to copy proven bestsellers rather than invent new ones. That second choice became the rule for everything that followed.
blocks.howStarted: As company histories tell the story, the first gown was cut and sewn at his sister's kitchen table, with help from his brother and sister. His future wife, Rosalía Mera, and his sister-in-law Primitiva Renedo did much of the early sewing. His very first customer was his former employer. After that he sold dressing gowns, housecoats and lingerie to other shops in A Coruña. By 1963 he had saved enough to open his first small factory.
blocks.funding: Personal savings, and the exact sum is disputed. Ortega told his biographer that he and his brother Antonio opened GOA's bank account with 2,500 pesetas. Forbes and a company history say he started with 5,000 pesetas, which they put at about $25. There were no investors and no bank round recorded in any source we found.
blocks.whatHappened: GOA grew into a real manufacturer. Until 1975 it mostly made clothes for other people's shops, but it already had several workshops and was selling outside Spain. One supplier shows how big it got: a textile factory called Fibracolor, in Tordera near Barcelona, ended up making about 90% of its output for GOA. A 2025 history of Zara says that dependence ultimately doomed the plant. GOA itself became part of the group that was later renamed Inditex.
blocks.lesson: Your first customer can be the person who already trusts you, even your old boss. But be careful about dependence: a customer or supplier that relies on one buyer for 90% of its work is fragile.

blocks.text: His first customer was his old boss. Think about that.

For twelve years Ortega was a maker, not a seller. He knew factories, fabrics and costs, but other people owned the counter where customers paid. In 1975 he crossed that counter. The move from manufacturer to retailer is the single biggest decision in this whole book.

blocks.name: Zara
blocks.idea: A shop that sold low-priced versions of popular, more expensive fashion. The first clothes used cheap fabrics like polyester and viscose. Prices were rock-bottom, margins were thin, and the plan was to sell fast.
blocks.decision: Owning the shop meant he could control the whole chain: design, make and sell. If a style sold, his own workshops could make more; if it flopped, he could stop. The name was nearly different. He wanted to call it Zorba, after the film Zorba the Greek, but that name clashed with an existing business, so the letters were rearranged into Zara.
blocks.howStarted: The first Zara opened on ==9 May 1975== at numbers 64–66 of Juan Flórez Street in A Coruña. He opened it with his then-wife, Rosalía Mera. Ortega was 39. A second store followed on Torreiro Street in the same city. In 1976 the business was incorporated as Goasam and more Zara shops opened across Spain.
blocks.funding: The shop grew out of GOA's own business; there is no record of outside backers. Even when the company listed on the stock market in 2001, it was still almost entirely owned by Ortega, his relatives and its managers.
blocks.whatHappened: By the end of the 1980s there were more than 80 Zaras in Spain. The chain went abroad in 1988, and by 2001 it had 450 stores in 29 countries. In the first half of 2026, the Zara segment (Zara, Zara Home and Lefties together) sold €13.78 billion. The very first store closed on 30 January 2026, more than fifty years after it opened, because Inditex said it was too small for the large modern stores the brand now builds.
blocks.lesson: Control of both the factory and the shop let him change what he sold in weeks, not seasons. Owning the customer relationship is worth more than owning the machines.

blocks.text: As Zara grew, Ortega needed a parent company to hold the shops, factories and new chains. A holding company is simply a company whose main job is to own other companies. His was called Industria de Diseño Textil, or Inditex for short.

blocks.name: Inditex (Industria de Diseño Textil)
blocks.idea: One parent company to run Zara, its factories and every future brand as a single system, with shared design, logistics and computers.
blocks.decision: In 1984 he hired José María Castellano, a computer expert, to build a system linking stores to factories. In 1985 the group took the name Inditex. In 2001 he made the biggest structural decision of his life: he sold part of his shares to the public on the Madrid Stock Exchange.
blocks.howStarted: Inditex was formally founded in 1985 to bring all the group's companies under one banner. In 2000 it moved into a new headquarters in Arteixo, just outside A Coruña, where it still is.
blocks.funding: No outside investors were needed. When Inditex listed in 2001, Forbes reported that none of the roughly $2 billion raised would go to the company itself: it went to Ortega and a few relatives who sold shares. The shares started trading on 23 May 2001.
blocks.whatHappened: In the year to 31 January 2026, Inditex sold €39.9 billion of clothes and earned €6.2 billion in net income. It had 5,460 stores, sold in 214 markets, made €10.7 billion of sales online, and had €11 billion of net cash. Six months later, at 31 July 2026, it had 5,444 stores and €10.4 billion of net cash. Ortega still owns about 59% of it.
blocks.lesson: A stock market listing does not have to be about raising money. Inditex used it to put a public price on the shares and build a structure that could outlive its founder.

blocks.text: His IPO raised zero new money for the company. Read that again.

Then came the clever part. Instead of making Zara bigger and bigger for everyone, Inditex built separate chains for separate customers. Each new brand had its own style, its own shops and its own price level, but all of them used the same back-office machine in Galicia.

blocks.name: Pull&Bear
blocks.idea: Casual, 'urban' fashion, sold in its own shops under its own name.
blocks.decision: Instead of stretching the Zara name, Inditex gave this style a separate name and separate shops.
blocks.howStarted: Launched by Inditex in 1991 as a casual chain. By the early 2000s it had about 300 stores in nearly 20 countries.
blocks.funding: Built inside Inditex with the group's own money. The company did not publish the start-up cost.
blocks.whatHappened: It is still one of the group's core chains. In the first half of 2026, Pull&Bear sold €1.26 billion, up almost 9% on a year earlier.
blocks.lesson: A new customer group often needs a new brand, not a stretched old one.

blocks.name: Massimo Dutti
blocks.idea: A ready-made fashion chain with its own established style, which Inditex could buy instead of build.
blocks.decision: This time Inditex did not build from scratch. It bought into an existing brand, taking 65% in 1991 and buying the rest in 1995.
blocks.howStarted: Massimo Dutti already existed as a separate company when Inditex bought its first stake in 1991. Under Inditex it grew to nearly 300 stores in 23 countries by the early 2000s.
blocks.funding: Paid for by Inditex. The purchase prices were not disclosed in any source we could check.
blocks.whatHappened: In 2021 Inditex folded the Uterqüe brand into it, because Massimo Dutti was already strong in the US, Canada, Mexico and Turkey. In the first half of 2026, Massimo Dutti sold €988 million, up about 10%.
blocks.lesson: Buying a stake first and the rest later is a cheap way to learn before you commit.

blocks.text: Not every early idea lasted. In the early 1990s Inditex ran a children's chain called Kiddy's Class as a sub-brand of Zara. It is not among the group's brands today. The group also needed somewhere to sell clothes that did not sell at full price, and that problem created a brand of its own.

blocks.name: Lefties
blocks.idea: An outlet for unsold Zara stock, so leftover clothes made money instead of sitting in warehouses.
blocks.decision: Over time Inditex turned it from a clearance shop into a standalone low-price brand aimed at Gen Z shoppers. That puts it head to head with Shein and Primark.
blocks.howStarted: It began as an outlet for Zara's leftovers. Sources disagree on the exact year it started (see the fact-check notes).
blocks.funding: Built inside Inditex; costs not published.
blocks.whatHappened: Inditex planned to open 200 new Lefties stores in major Western European countries in 2026, including the UK and France, as part of a €1.8 billion investment plan for 2025–2026. Its sales are reported inside the Zara segment.
blocks.lesson: Your waste can become a product. A clearance channel can grow into a weapon against cheaper rivals.

blocks.name: Bershka
blocks.idea: Fashion for young women, in its own chain of shops.
blocks.decision: Inditex built a separate chain aimed at young women rather than adding a section to Zara.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in 1998. Within about six years it had more than 200 stores in 11 countries.
blocks.funding: Built inside Inditex with the group's own money; costs not published.
blocks.whatHappened: It is now the group's second-biggest chain by sales. In the first half of 2026 it sold €1.68 billion, up 16.7%.
blocks.lesson: The youngest customers move fastest. A system built for speed suits them best.

blocks.name: Stradivarius
blocks.idea: Another youth fashion chain, with its own look.
blocks.decision: A year after launching Bershka, Inditex bought an existing youth chain instead of building another one. Stradivarius was already selling in nine countries.
blocks.howStarted: Stradivarius was an existing company when Inditex bought it in 1999.
blocks.funding: Paid for by Inditex. The price was not disclosed in any reliable source we found.
blocks.whatHappened: It became one of the group's fastest growers. In the first half of 2026 it sold €1.57 billion, up 18.5%.
blocks.lesson: Sometimes buying a rival is cheaper and faster than fighting it.

blocks.name: Oysho
blocks.decision: In a way, this was a return home. Forbes says Ortega's first business in 1963 was a lingerie and sleepwear business. Thirty-eight years later his group launched a whole chain for the same category.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in 2001, the same year Inditex listed on the stock market.
blocks.funding: Built inside Inditex; costs not published.
blocks.whatHappened: In the first half of 2026 Oysho sold €472 million. Its growth rate, 21.3%, was the fastest of any Inditex chain in that period.
blocks.lesson: Old skills come back. What you learned in your first business can power a later one.

blocks.name: Zara Home
blocks.idea: Bedding, tableware and home accessories, sold with the same fast-changing approach as Zara's clothes.
blocks.decision: This was Inditex's first move beyond clothes, and it carried the Zara name into the new category.
blocks.funding: Built inside Inditex; costs not published.
blocks.whatHappened: It is still running. Inditex now reports it together with Zara and Lefties.
blocks.lesson: A strong brand name can carry you into a new category, if the promise to customers stays the same.

blocks.text: Now the failures. Nobody puts these on posters.

blocks.name: Often
blocks.idea: A chain for men aged 20 to 45, with a more classic look than Pull&Bear. It started as an offshoot of Pull&Bear.
blocks.decision: Inditex wanted a piece of the adult men's market. In September 2006 it made the opposite decision and pulled the plug, calling the move an adaptation to market trends.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in 2003 and grew to about 40 stores.
blocks.funding: Built inside Inditex; costs not published.
blocks.whatHappened: Results were poor, and the brand never built a personality as clear as the other chains. In September 2006 Inditex closed it. Of its 40 stores, 30 were handed to another company, Friday's Project, and 10 were reused by Zara, Pull&Bear and Massimo Dutti. A Banesto report cited by Reuters said the chain made up less than 1% of the group, so the share price barely noticed. It was the first project Inditex had ever closed since Zara began in 1975.
blocks.lesson: Kill a weak brand early, while it is small. Because Inditex did not own the shops (it rented them), closing Often was mostly a property deal, not a disaster.

blocks.name: Uterqüe
blocks.idea: Inditex's first premium concept: accessories, and later women's clothing, at higher prices than its other chains.
blocks.decision: The bet was that the Inditex machine could also sell upmarket handbags and accessories. After 13 years the group decided it could reach more customers by putting the range inside Massimo Dutti, which was already strong in the US, Canada, Mexico and Turkey.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in July 2008 with three stores opening at once, in A Coruña, Madrid and Barcelona. By the end of its first year it had 31 stores in three countries. A short-lived men's line was dropped.
blocks.funding: Built inside Inditex; costs not published.
blocks.whatHappened: It stayed the smallest chain in the group. In the first half of 2021 it sold €48 million from 82 stores. In September 2021 Inditex announced that Uterqüe would be merged into Massimo Dutti, and its own stores closed in early 2022. One Spanish business magazine called it Ortega's 'first big failure'. Its products never really caught on in a market crowded with established brands.
blocks.lesson: A system built for cheap, fast fashion does not automatically work for premium goods. Know where your machine's strength ends.

blocks.text: By 2021 Ortega was receiving more than a billion euros a year in dividends. A dividend is a share of the company's profit paid out in cash to the people who own its shares. He did not spend that money on more fashion brands. He put it into a private company called Pontegadea.

blocks.name: Pontegadea (property empire)
blocks.idea: Buy prime buildings in big cities that already have long leases with strong tenants, so they pay rent from day one.
blocks.decision: Rather than gamble his dividends on start-ups or more retail, he chose bricks: offices, shops, hotels and warehouses. His tenants include Apple, Amazon, Google, Spotify and Walmart.
blocks.howStarted: Pontegadea is his family investment company. It holds his Inditex shares and runs his property business. Its buildings are spread across cities such as Madrid, London, New York, Paris, Tokyo and Vancouver.
blocks.funding: Inditex dividends. In 2021, Pontegadea's income was €1.97 billion: €1.29 billion from Inditex dividends, €647 million from rent, and €29 million from other stakes.
blocks.whatHappened: The property portfolio was worth €15.3 billion at the end of 2021 and about €22 billion by 2025. In London alone it owns around 14 buildings worth over €4.2 billion, including the Adelphi Building (home of The Economist, bought in 2018 for about €680 million) and the Post Building (home of McKinsey, bought in 2019 for about €700 million). For 2025, Spanish press counted at least 10 property deals worth more than €1.65 billion, while Forbes counted 13 worth over $3 billion. In April 2026, Forbes called him the world's richest real estate baron.
blocks.lesson: When your main business throws off cash, put it into something that does not rise and fall with that business.

blocks.name: Pontegadea (energy, telecom and ports stakes)
blocks.idea: Own minority stakes in 'boring' infrastructure: gas pipelines, power grids, telecom towers, wind farms and ports. These businesses earn steady fees for decades.
blocks.decision: He chose stakes, not control. Its stakes have ranged from about 5% to 49%, leaving the day-to-day running to specialist operators.
blocks.howStarted: By 2021 Pontegadea held 5% of Enagás, Spain's gas-network operator, and 30% of Telxius, a telecom-infrastructure company controlled by Telefónica. In 2021 it bought 5% of Redeia (Spain's power-grid operator), 12% of REN (Portugal's grid operator) and 49% of a Repsol wind-farm portfolio, its first renewable-energy deal.
blocks.funding: Inditex dividends and cash held by Pontegadea, which had net cash of €1.08 billion at the end of 2021.
blocks.whatHappened: In January 2021 Telxius sold about 30,722 mobile-phone tower sites to American Tower for €7.7 billion in cash; Pontegadea booked a gain of about €331 million. In 2025 it bought 49% of the British ports group PD Ports from Brookfield. In August 2026 it closed a deal with Macquarie and UniSuper for Australia's Qube, valued at about A$11.7 billion, taking a 15% stake.
blocks.lesson: Steady, regulated businesses are a good home for money you cannot afford to lose.

blocks.text: Fashion is risky. Power grids are not. He owns both.

Line them all up and you see a clear shape. A workshop paid for a shop. The shop paid for a chain. The chain paid for new brands, and the brands paid dividends that bought buildings and power lines. __Two of the brands failed, but both were closed fast and cheaply, before they could hurt the core.__

In the 1970s and 80s, clothing companies worked slowly. A new collection could take up to six months to go from design to shop. That meant most brands could only launch two or three collections a year. They had to guess, months in advance, what people would want to wear.

Ortega hated guessing. He wanted what one company history calls 'instant fashions': clothes that reacted to what customers were buying right now. Because he owned both factories and shops, he could do something rivals could not. He could see what sold on Monday and start making more of it on Tuesday.

The tool that made this possible arrived in 1984. Ortega hired José María Castellano, a computer expert who had worked in the IT department of the insurer Aegon in Spain and as finance chief of a Spanish food company. Castellano built a computer system that linked the shops to the factories. Sales data flowed back to headquarters, and new orders flowed out. Design-to-shop time fell to ==10 to 15 days==.
He hired a computer expert in 1984. Remember the year.

Speed changed how people shopped. Zara restocked so often that the whole range turned over about every two weeks. In some cities, the day new stock arrived became known as 'Z-day'. __Scarcity became the marketing: if you liked something, you bought it now, because it might be gone next week.__

Forbes compared Zara with its rivals just before the 2001 listing. Zara needed about three weeks from approving a design to delivering it to shops. H&M and Gap needed three to five months. No Zara model stayed on sale longer than four weeks. And because it made only what sold, its stock of finished clothes was 7% of revenue, against 13% at H&M.

The system also had a human side that is easy to forget. In 2001 about half of Zara's goods were made in-house. Much of the sewing was done by around 350 outside workshops in Galicia and northern Portugal, employing roughly 11,000 mostly informal workers. Inditex did not own those workshops. Forbes estimated that a seamstress might earn about $500 a month, less than half the average Spanish industrial wage, and warned that tighter rules could raise costs.
Cheap and fast always has a cost. Ask who pays it.

Zara did something else unusual: it spent almost nothing on advertising. The money went into shops in the best streets, and into making those shops look perfect. In Arteixo, Inditex even kept an underground lab with about 25 full-size shop windows, so it could test displays under different kinds of light before copying them around the world.
He is very hands-on about the designs.

blocks.text: Ortega stayed close to the product and far from the cameras. He gave no interviews, held no launch parties, and was known for turning up unannounced where something had gone wrong. No photograph of him was published until 1999. While other fashion founders became celebrities, he stayed almost invisible.
Going abroad, one city at a time

By the end of the 1980s there were more than 80 Zaras in Spain. The first store outside Spain opened in 1988, just across the border in Porto, Portugal. Then came two very different tests: New York in 1989 and Paris in 1990.

Paris welcomed Zara. America was harder. By the early 2000s, more than a decade after arriving, Zara still had only six stores in the US. __Not every market rewards the same formula, and Ortega was willing to grow slowly where it was not working.__

Inditex also learned to expand without always paying for everything itself. In Japan in 1997 it used a joint venture, which means a company co-owned with a local partner. From 1998 it also used franchises in places like the Middle East. A franchise is when a local company runs the shops under your brand and pays you for the right to do so.

blocks.text: By 2000 Inditex made a net profit of about $230 million on $2.3 billion of sales, roughly triple its profit five years earlier. Its profit margin was higher than H&M's or Gap's. A small family firm from a corner of north-west Spain had built a supply chain that the biggest names in fashion could not match.

In 2001 Ortega was 65 and controlled almost all of Inditex. He decided to sell part of it to the public. This is called an IPO, or initial public offering: the first time a company sells its shares on a stock exchange, so that anyone can buy a piece of it.
Inditex's shares started trading in Madrid on ==23 May 2001== at €14.70 each, which valued the company at about €9.2 billion.
Demand was huge. The price jumped straight away by more than 26%, then slipped back to about 21% above the launch price by the afternoon. Ortega's stake fell to about 60%.

Here is the surprising part. Forbes reported that none of the roughly $2 billion raised went to the company. All of it went to Ortega and a few relatives who sold shares. Forbes estimated the expected price at about 35 times Inditex's yearly profit. That ratio, called the price-to-earnings ratio, shows how much buyers are willing to pay today for each euro of profit; a high number means they expect fast growth.
He was 65 when he went public. Not every founder is young.

The listing made him Spain's richest man, with a fortune of more than €4.6 billion. It also forced the most private man in Spanish business to be more open, because listed companies must publish their accounts and their main owners. __An IPO is a trade: you get a public price for your shares, and the public gets to look inside.__
Growing faster than ever

After the listing, Inditex sped up. In 2003 alone it opened more than 360 stores, and by mid-2004 it had passed 2,000. Sales in 2003 reached about €4.6 billion, with Zara bringing in roughly three-quarters. In 2002 it began building a second big logistics centre, in Zaragoza.

Not every bet worked. In 2003 the group launched Often, a chain for adult men. By September 2006 it had closed all 40 stores. It was the first project Inditex had ever shut. Because the shops were rented, the group handed most of them to another retailer and reused the rest.
Handing over the keys

Ortega also started to step back from daily management. In 2005 Castellano left as chief executive, and Pablo Isla took over. Isla ran Inditex for about 17 years. During his first decade, the store count grew from 2,692 to more than 7,000. By the time he left, the group's sales were about 500% higher than when he started.

In 2011 Ortega gave up the chairman's job too, and Isla took it over. Ortega kept his shares, but he no longer ran the company. __He separated owning the business from running it, years before he had to.__
Very important for founders: hand over before you're forced to.
Zara comes to India

In 2010 Zara opened its first stores in India: one in Select Citywalk mall in Delhi, and one soon after in Palladium mall in Mumbai. The stores were huge, over 16,000 square feet. Prices were set close to Zara's prices in Singapore and Dubai, which made it cheaper than many imported rivals like Mango and Esprit.

Industry sources told Forbes India that Zara's Delhi store sold close to ₹1.25 crore in its first weekend, with Mumbai nearly the same. Footfall at Select Citywalk rose about 40%. Fresh stock arrived every few days, flown in from Spain twice a week.

The same article listed the risks honestly. India has less seasonal change, shoppers replace their wardrobes less often, and many prefer traditional wear and brighter colours. One expert said local sourcing would only make sense once Zara had about 100 stores. The lesson for founders: even a winning formula must be tested against local habits.
Briefly the richest person on Earth

As Inditex's share price climbed, so did Ortega's fortune. In March 2013 Forbes named him the year's biggest winner, worth $57 billion. Then, on 23 October 2015, he briefly passed Bill Gates to become the world's richest man. It happened again in September 2016 and, for part of one day, on 29 August 2017.

blocks.text: The copying problem

A model built on copying popular styles fast has a weak point: sometimes the style belongs to someone small. In July 2016, illustrator Tuesday Bassen said Zara had used four of her original artworks, and at least a dozen independent artists made similar claims. Inditex said it took such claims very seriously, investigated, and suspended the items from sale while it worked with her lawyers.

That episode shows the other side of 'fast'. The same speed that lets Zara react to trends can also let it react to someone else's work before anyone checks. For a young founder, the takeaway is clear: build checks into your speed, or your best feature becomes your biggest legal risk.

chapters.title: The Year the Shops Went Dark

blocks.text: Inditex had made a profit every single quarter since it listed in 2001. Then came the spring of 2020. As Covid-19 spread, governments ordered shops to close. At the worst point, up to 88% of Inditex's stores were shut. Of nearly 7,500 shops, only 965 were open during the lockdown.
For a company whose whole model was physical shops in busy streets, this was a nightmare. In the three months from February to April 2020, sales fell 44%, from €5.9 billion to €3.
3 billion. Inditex reported a net loss of ==€409 million==, against a profit of €734 million a year earlier. It was its first loss since going public.
Nineteen years of profits as a listed company. Then one virus.

Part of that loss was a choice. Inditex booked a €308 million provision, which is money set aside in the accounts for a cost the company knows is coming. In this case it was for closing and reshaping stores, a plan that had started before the virus. The dividend was also suspended in March.

Then Inditex turned the crisis into a reset. It announced it would close 1,000 to 1,200 smaller, older stores over two years, mostly from brands other than Zara. It would spend an extra €2.7 billion between 2020 and 2022, about €1 billion of it on online selling. Online sales had already grown 50% in the quarter, and 95% in April alone.
total confidence in our business model
blocks.who: Pablo Isla, Inditex chairman, June 2020

blocks.text: The bet was that fewer, bigger, better stores would work hand in hand with online shopping. Online had been 14% of sales in 2019; the target was more than 25% by 2022. __The pandemic did not change the plan. It forced Inditex to do faster what it had already decided to do.__

Look at the result. Inditex had 7,412 stores when the pandemic hit. At the end of its 2025 financial year it had 5,460, nearly 2,000 fewer. Yet that year it sold €39.9 billion, including €10.7 billion online, and earned €6.2 billion.
Cutting the losers

The reset also claimed a brand. In September 2021 Inditex announced that Uterqüe, its upmarket accessories chain, would be merged into Massimo Dutti. Its own shops, about 80 of them, closed in early 2022. Inditex said the move would let the products reach Massimo Dutti's stronger markets in North America and Turkey.
Walking away from Russia

In March 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, Inditex closed its more than 500 shops in Russia. It set aside €216 million to cover the cost of winding down its business there. In October 2022 it agreed to sell the Russian business to the Daher Group, which runs the retailer Azadea, Zara's partner in the Middle East since 1998.

The deal moved most of the store leases to the buyer and was meant to keep a substantial number of jobs. Inditex also did not rule out returning one day if circumstances changed. It is a good example of exiting carefully: take the loss, protect people where you can, and do not burn every bridge.
A clean exit is a skill. Learn it.
The next generation

On 1 April 2022, Pablo Isla left. Ortega's daughter Marta Ortega Pérez became chair of Inditex, and Óscar García Maceiras, who had become chief executive, ran the company day to day. The founder, then 86, remained the controlling shareholder through Pontegadea.

blocks.text: Most people imagine billionaires get rich by selling their company. Ortega mostly did the opposite: he kept it. As of 2026 he still controls 59.29% of Inditex, through two companies: Pontegadea Inversiones, which owns 50.01%, and Partler, which owns 9.
28%. Inditex has about 3.12 billion shares, so his stake is roughly 1.85 billion shares.
Every year, Inditex pays part of its profit to shareholders. For its 2025 financial year it paid €1.75 per share: €1.20 as an ordinary dividend and €0.55 as a 'bonus' dividend.
The money arrives in two halves, on 4 May and 2 November 2026. For Ortega that adds up to a record of about ==€3.23 billion== this year, up from about €3.1 billion the year before.
The second half, €0.875 a share, was set for payment on 2 November 2026. On Ortega's roughly 1.85 billion shares, that comes to about €1.6 billion by our arithmetic, in a single payment.
€1.6 billion in one day. Without selling a single share.
That cash has grown fast. In 2021 Ortega's dividends from Inditex were about €1.29 billion. In 2022 they were expected to be about €1.
72 billion. By 2026 they had passed €3.2 billion. __When a business keeps growing its profits, its owner's income grows with it, every year, without ever selling.__
Where the dividends go

Forbes says Ortega reinvests most of his dividends in property across Europe and North America. Pontegadea's strategy is simple: buy buildings in prime locations that already have long leases with strong tenants, so the rent starts flowing immediately. It is the opposite of a start-up bet.
The numbers show how big this second engine has become. At the end of 2021 the property portfolio was worth €15.3 billion. By 2025 it was about €22 billion.
In the UK alone, Pontegadea's property company valued its buildings at about £2.7 billion at the end of 2025, and its profit more than doubled to £70.1 million.

blocks.text: In 2021, when the accounts were broken down clearly, Pontegadea's income was €1.97 billion. About two-thirds came from Inditex dividends and about one-third from rent. It made a net profit of €1.
6 billion that year and moved from net debt to €1.08 billion of net cash. In other words, even with all those buildings, it held more cash than debt.

The group keeps growing. Filings for 2025 show the main Pontegadea companies together held assets of about €117 billion and made a profit of about €10 billion. These are the same companies that hold his Inditex shares, so the totals largely reflect the fashion business rather than separate wealth.
The co-founder's share

Ortega was not the only person made rich by Zara. Rosalía Mera, his first wife and co-founder of the first store, held 6.99% of Inditex, according to Madrid stock exchange filings. When she died in August 2013 at 69, Forbes estimated her fortune at $6.1 billion, making her Spain's richest woman and the world's richest self-made woman on its list.
A seamstress who co-founded a shop. She died a billionaire.
How the fortune adds up today

On 2 November 2026, Forbes's real-time list put Ortega's net worth at $147.8 billion, ranking him 12th in the world. The biggest part is his Inditex stake. The second is the property and infrastructure empire built from its dividends, which in April 2026 led Forbes to call him the world's richest real estate baron.
Look at how that wealth was built. He started with his own savings, not investors' money. The only big sale of his shares in this story came at the IPO, when he was 65.

He kept control, kept the profits flowing, and used the cash to build a second, safer engine. __The fortune did not come from one lucky deal. It came from owning a cash machine for fifty years and never selling it.__
