blocks.text: There is one more lesson hidden here. Ortega's biggest financial decisions were mostly about what not to do: not taking outside money, not selling control, not spending his dividends on flashy new ventures. For a founder, saying no to the wrong money can matter as much as saying yes to the right idea.

Mid-morning at the Inditex headquarters in Arteixo, a security guard warns his colleagues: “The boss is coming in.” A black Mercedes pulls up. The passenger sits in the front, next to the driver, in a white shirt with no tie and a dark jacket. In 2013, when one Spanish reporter described this scene, that passenger was the third-richest man on Earth.

Nobody jumps up when he walks in. He does not head for a grand room with a view. He walks into a huge hall full of designers, talks to whoever is there, and argues about shapes and colours. __He runs the company the way a shop assistant runs a shop floor: standing up, looking, asking.__
Third-richest man alive. Sits in the front seat.
A desk among the designers

Fortune reported in 2013 that he sat at a plain desk at the end of the open workspace of Zara Woman, the women's fashion team, and said flatly that he had never had an office. The Economist went further in 2016: no office, no desk, no desktop computer. German business magazine manager magazin called it management by walking around. He wanders through the building, asks questions, and now and then writes on a small notepad.

__Staff say you can simply stop him and ask.__ Newer employees told Fortune they were amazed by how often he discussed colours and trends with them. Loreta García had joined straight out of design school 23 years earlier and ran Zara Woman's trends department. She described a place where the founder was as easy to reach as the person at the next table.
You can ask Ortega, ‘What do you think of this?’ It's very flexible. You don't have to fix an appointment.
blocks.who: Loreta García, head of trends at Zara Woman, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: His day, as far as anyone has reported it

His daily routine is known only in pieces. In 2008, at 72, he had given himself one luxury, his biographer Covadonga O'Shea said: he now reached work at ==11 in the morning instead of 9==. Before that he went to the gym and had breakfast with friends. Fortune reported in 2013 that the breakfast was with acquaintances at a local businessmen's club, and that friends said it was eggs and fries.

The work itself ran long. CNBC reported that he once went 25 years without a holiday, and manager magazin said that even in old age he often stayed in the design hall until late evening. Yet he protected his sleep. Reading notes on O'Shea's book record him saying he needs at least eight hours.

items.label: his trip from town to headquarters, reported as a daily habit even at 80
needed to ask him a question, staff told Fortune in 2013
what warehouse staff paid for a canteen meal in 2015, whatever their salary

blocks.text: Talk, not memos

José María Castellano was chief executive of Inditex for years and worked beside him for decades. He told The Economist how the boss operates: intense talks in small groups, paperwork handed to others, hard listening, and speech over writing. People close to Ortega said he reads novels and newspapers but is uneasy writing at length. Fortune put it simply: he prefers touching fabrics to reading memos.

A man who left school in his early teens built a giant company around that fact instead of hiding it. A question he often asks is short, O'Shea writes: “What is this for?” He is not a man for long technical speeches. __He designed the company around what he was good at, and hired people for the rest.__
Bad at writing memos? Fine. Be great at something else.
How decisions get made

Zara does not leave decisions to one star designer. Fortune described commercial specialists sitting right beside the designers, reading store managers' sales reports to see what is selling and, more telling, what customers are asking for. Nobody on that floor is expected to guess alone.

El País was let into the Zara design hall in 2013 and watched this happen. Four women stood at a table with fabric, pencil sketches and a sales list, deciding how large a flower print should be. One of them was a saleswoman who knew the numbers for any item at any store. None of them would give a surname, because egos are not welcome there.
We all have an opinion. We are customers of our own business.
blocks.who: Loreto, a Zara designer, to El País (2013)

blocks.text: His own calls can be small and fast. On one visit to a test shop inside headquarters, he saw a very sophisticated lamp in a window display. He asked for it to be taken away, because it looked showy and did not fit Zara. O'Shea says he would not let it pass.

There is a famous story, told by Fortune with the words “as the story goes”. Ortega's car stops at a red light in La Coruña. He sees a young biker in a patched denim jacket, phones an aide, describes the stitching, the shape and the colour, and ends with one word: “¡Hácedla!” Make it.
Treat this one as legend. The habit behind it is real.
Letting go

Ortega knows what he cannot do. Manager magazin listed the weak spots he is well aware of: strategy, finance and logistics. He handed those to Castellano and later to Pablo Isla. Because his English is poor, which he deeply regrets, he trusted the international expansion to an executive named Fernando Martínez.

Letting go did not come naturally. In O'Shea's book he says he used to give an opinion on everything, and that giving up the commercial side was hard, but he had to. __His rule now is that when he delegates he trusts fully, while making sure people know they are not alone.__ On his favourite walk through the design area, he says he mostly listens.
It teaches me a lot to listen to them and, if they ask my opinion, I give it, but they are good professionals and know very well what they are doing.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, in O'Shea's book (translated from Spanish)

blocks.text: Who gets hired, and who stays
Inditex tends to grow its own people. “We all started here young and have grown up with Ortega,” Loreta García said of the directors.

__But the two biggest hires were outsiders chosen for skills he lacked.__ Pablo Isla came in 2005, aged 41, from the tobacco group Altadis, on Castellano's own recommendation. Ortega's verdict on him was that he rolls up his sleeves and treats no job as beneath him.

Family is also part of the picture. Vanity Fair España reported in 2018 that two of his wife's brothers held senior roles running Zara and Massimo Dutti, and a brother-in-law was Zara's general manager until 2011. His daughter Marta started on a shop floor in London. We found no on-the-record account of how Ortega personally fires people, so we will not guess. O'Shea calls him warm and demanding, and nobody who knows him told manager magazin he had ever raised his voice.
What it is like to work there

Staff describe something fast and flat. Designers produce about three items a day, and Fortune called the pace frantic. Suits and ties are rare. People say “going to the factory” when they mean going to the head office. Isla's description of Ortega's legacy was: “The entrepreneurial spirit, the self-criticism, the culture: The company is completely flat.”

__The canteen is where the legend gets tested.__ Warehouse staff at Zara's logistics arm paid 15 cents for a meal valued at €3.80, and in 2015 workers said the founder still showed up to eat there. The same report quoted the works council president, Luis Leis of the CGT union, complaining that the canteens were often overwhelmed. Until a 2014 labour deal, night-shift workers got by on a cold sandwich.
We knew Amancio well. He was very close to the workers.
blocks.who: Mercedes López, who joined at 14 and became textile union representative at Inditex, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: He proudly tells O'Shea about Luis, a warehouse director who had a heart attack at work. As the ambulance was called, Luis asked for a phone so his deputy could cover his job at once. “That is what my people are like,” Ortega says.
Inspiring, or a warning? Your health outranks any warehouse. Think about it.

Ortega has written almost nothing and said very little in public. So his beliefs have to be pieced together from one authorised book, a few annual report letters and a talk to business professors. The surprise is how consistent they are. Here are seven, each with the story behind it.
1. The shop tells you what to make

As a teenage shop hand, he had no say in what the store bought. __All he could do was watch what customers liked, and he later called that his education.__ Then he saw the same problem from the other side. O'Shea's book says that when he sold to the department store El Corte Inglés, buyers asked for things that did not match what shoppers actually wanted. That pushed him towards opening his own stores.
The customer has always driven the business model.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, Inditex's 2009 annual report, via CNBC

blocks.text: O'Shea offers a sharp example. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, she says, she spent days in New York that Christmas and found that bright collections had stalled, while Zara's fast system had filled its shops with dark, sober tones.
Your teacher is whoever is about to buy. Watch them.
2. Never be satisfied

In 2007 he told a group of business professors what he thought was most dangerous for a company. Spain's Cinco Días reported it, and CNBC later retold it. He did not name a rival or a recession. __He named feeling good about yourself.__
Complacency is the worst. I never allow myself to be content with what I have done, and I have always tried to instill this in everyone around me.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, to business professors in 2007, via CNBC

blocks.text: O'Shea's book carries a stronger version: blind optimism is negative, and to succeed you must turn an organisation upside down every day. He also said: “We have never relaxed or accepted an easy success. Optimism can be very negative. You have to take risks!” This from a man whose company grew sales by 17% in the first nine months of 2012, when Spain had ==24% unemployment==.
3. Build what can't be copied

Rivals have tried hard to catch up. Fortune reported in 2013 that Tadashi Yanai, the founder of Uniqlo, had made beating Zara his stated goal in life. When the fashion company Esprit named Inditex's former distribution and operations manager as its new chief executive, its shares rose 28% that day. Investors were paying for one person who had seen the machine from inside.
Very few companies can challenge Inditex at this time. The company is in a race with themselves rather than anything else.
blocks.who: Christodoulos Chaviaras, retail analyst at Barclays Capital, to Fortune (2013)

blocks.text: __A secret can be stolen in an afternoon. A system built over 40 years cannot.__ Speed was the core of it from the 1970s, when he set a rule that stores must get orders within 48 hours. That rule alone decided where the first Zara shops could open: near La Coruña, many along the truck route to Barcelona's textile factories.
Could a rival copy your startup after a one-week visit? Be honest.
4. Good clothes should not be a privilege

As a young shop manager, he noticed that only a few wealthy residents could afford the clothes he sold, so he started making cheaper versions. Looking back, he described that ambition in terms much bigger than fashion.
Yo quería ser un empresario diferente, cambiar socialmente el mundo.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, in O'Shea's book (publisher's extract)

blocks.text: That means: I wanted to be a different kind of businessman, to change the world socially. He also has a theory about why people buy from him. __Most people, he says, will not spend much on clothes, and even wealthy people he knows spend least on labels.__ On Zara itself, he gave O'Shea a sentence that sounds nothing like fashion marketing: “For me it is serenity, not spectacle.”
5. Treat people as the point

Ortega's word for this is one you rarely hear from a chief executive. “Loving the people who work with us is an obligation,” he told O'Shea. A former HR director of Inditex recalled that his advice boiled down to two words: love people.

O'Shea has heard him say many times that being a businessman just to get rich is not worth it. __When he talks about scale, he talks in people.__ “We are 80,000 people,” he reminded her in 2008, “and you have to add all those who have worked in the company and are no longer here.” The chapter on what went wrong shows where this belief ran into hard limits, far from Galicia.
Nice words. The test is how you treat the furthest worker.
6. Fear stops you, so face the problem

O'Shea said in 2008 that neither the future nor the financial crisis seemed to worry him. He believes fear paralyses you and that the job is to confront what is in front of you. He gave the professors a related line in 2007.
If you want to innovate, don't focus on the results.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, 2007, via CNBC

blocks.text: He has a simple faith underneath this. “I have the absolute conviction that we all come into the world to fulfil a mission,” he says in the book. He also says he does not get worked up, because everything has its moment and its reason. He does his thinking while walking the Camino de Santiago, the old pilgrim route through Galicia, where he looks back at his life as an impossible dream.
7. Your job can be your university, but don't copy the gap

“My university is my profession,” Ortega says. It is an easy line to misuse. He left school in his early teens because his family needed money, and he adds in the same passage that he did not study enough and misses it now. He never said you should skip school.
I had no time to study because I worked 24 hours a day. What I regret most after so many years is not speaking English. I make up for the rest by listening a lot and learning from those around me.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, to Covadonga O'Shea, via Cinco Días (translated from Spanish)

blocks.text: Look at what he does with his money. His foundation has sent more than ==5,500 teenagers== from Spain to spend a school year in the US or Canada, since 2010. A man with no degree who regrets having no English pays for young people to get exactly that. __He compensated for missing education by listening; he did not pretend it did not matter.__
Not ‘drop out and win’. ‘Keep learning, whatever happens.’ Very different.

chapters.title: Chickens, Horses and a Small Circle

blocks.text: Ortega has spent his life keeping this chapter short, and we will respect that. What follows is only what has been publicly reported and matters to understanding him. He is a very private man who married twice, has three children, and has lived almost all his adult life in one city.
His mother and the nickname

The story of the shopkeeper refusing his mother credit is told earlier in this book. What came after is less known. His mother Josefa lived to 94, and he says his wife Flora went to see her every single day in her last years. He once flew her to Marbella in his own plane, and she looked at him and asked herself aloud whether this could really be her boy.

She called him “Choliño”, and his nephews still call him uncle Cholo. In O'Shea's notes he speaks of mothers as the base of a family, saying that when she is gone, something collapses at any age. For a man who gives almost nothing away, these are the warmest lines he has allowed in print.
Future richest man on Earth. To his mother, always ‘Choliño’.
Rosalía

He married Rosalía Mera in 1966. She was a seamstress and a co-founder in the earliest days of the business, and they had two children, Sandra and a son. Their son was born with a severe disability. Mera later spoke publicly about what that meant, in words that do not need our help.
The transcendent change was the birth of my son. Finding yourself with a child who is not the one you were expecting is very hard.
blocks.who: Rosalía Mera, via El Confidencial (translated from Spanish)

blocks.text: They split in 1986, and she stepped back from day-to-day work, though she stayed on the board until 2004. She went back to study, founded the Paideia Foundation to help people with disabilities find a place in society, and became a rare outspoken voice among Spain's rich. She said of the split that anyone who claims a break-up leaves no mark is lying. She died in August 2013, aged 69, after a stroke on holiday in Menorca. Ortega attended the brief, simple ceremony, and El País noted that he drew the cameras even though he never says a word.
Flora and Marta

Flora Pérez Marcote worked inside his company, first in a factory cutting room and later running a Zara shop in Vigo. Their daughter Marta was born in 1984. The couple married in 2001 in the chapel of their country house, and were due to mark their silver wedding in May 2026. Flora sits on the Inditex board and chairs his foundation.

__Marta's path shows what he believes about learning a business.__ She graduated in London in 2007 and worked on a shop floor there, then moved through other countries and teams. She told The Wall Street Journal that in her first week she did not think she would survive it. El País reported that the company quietly protected her from photographers while she folded clothes. She became non-executive chair in April 2022.
Heir to a fortune, and she still started by folding clothes.
How he spends his time

__His pleasures are stubbornly ordinary.__ Fortune reports that he spends weekends at a country house, raising chickens and goats. ¡Hola! says the eggs and vegetables go on the family table. He devotes weeks each year to walking Galician pilgrim routes, and his lifelong dislike of flying has kept him close to home.

The one passion with a public face is horses. CNBC reported that he owns an equestrian centre in Finisterre, Galicia, where he rides. He also likes the gym and swimming. In 2016 he bought about 100 hectares in Galicia to plant native chestnut trees.
How he spends his money

His work clothes are plain. CNBC described grey slacks and an open-neck shirt, and a Spanish reporter saw a white shirt, no tie and a dark jacket. He does own a yacht, but the BBC noted in 2016 it was under 40 metres, modest beside his wealth. A spokesperson told the BBC that the scale of his success surprised him.

The big spending is elsewhere and it is quiet. Forbes counted about ==$24 billion== spent on 216 properties since 2001, and he has sold only a handful. Most of it is offices, hotels, shops and warehouses, not trophies. ¡Hola! reported that he planned to mark his 90th birthday with family and close friends, with no party and no tributes.
Plain shirt, chickens, 216 buildings. He spends on what lasts, not what shows.
Giving it away

His foundation dates from 2001, the year Inditex listed. For its first decade it worked mostly on education and social care. Then in October 2012, during Spain's economic crisis, it gave ==€20 million== to the charity Cáritas.
That was the largest private gift in Cáritas's 55-year history. __El País pointed out it was about 0.05% of his fortune, like someone with €10,000 giving €5.__

Medicine became the focus. From 2015 the foundation spent €310 million placing about 450 cancer diagnosis and radiotherapy machines in public hospitals across every Spanish region. In October 2021 it pledged €280 million for 10 proton therapy machines, a precise cancer treatment used especially for children and hard-to-reach tumours. Before that, Spain had only two such units, both private.

items.label: his 2024 contribution to the foundation, about 26.8% of that year's Inditex dividend
aid to people hit by the 2024 floods in Spain, through 40 town councils
seven public care homes in Galician cities, about 900 places, five delivered by 2026

blocks.text: When COVID hit Spain in March 2020, the group's supply chain became a public service. Inditex opened its China buying network and its cargo flights to the state. Its annual report counts 177 million items delivered on 66 flights, for public and private buyers. El Confidencial reported that the government used those flights free for half of what it bought at the peak. __The system he built for dresses turned out to work for ventilators too.__

__Not everyone cheers, and the criticism deserves a fair hearing.__ In 2021 Podemos, then in Spain's government, called the gift a publicity campaign. Its long-time leader Pablo Iglesias said on television that a decent democracy does not accept alms from millionaires. Xataka reported an estimate by the newspaper Público that the proton gift earned a tax benefit of €108 million to €123 million, which is legal.

The other complaint is timing. Four years on, El País noted in 2025, regions were still paying private hospitals because no donated machine was running yet. The foundation and the health ministry call the timetable reasonable for such complex projects.
Is it generosity or tax planning? It can be both. Decide for yourself.

Late in 1990, the editor of a Spanish fashion magazine toured Inditex's headquarters and met a strong man in shirtsleeves with a friendly smile. She and her colleague took him for the floor supervisor. They explained they were journalists invited by Mr Ortega. He answered in warm Galician slang: “Well, dears, here I am. I am Ortega.”

That editor was Covadonga O'Shea, and she would later write his only authorised biography. But the mistake was common. Even investors visiting before the 2001 stock market listing awkwardly confused him with other staff. No photograph of him was published until 1999.

José María Castellano used to tell this one. He was eating in a restaurant with Ortega when a businessman walked over to their table and said to Castellano: when you see Amancio, give him my regards, it has been ages. Ortega was sitting right there.
Imagine being that businessman, realising later who was at the table.
A choice, not an accident

__The hiding is deliberate.__ Castellano did the analyst meetings and investor talks for years, and Ortega stayed away from the ceremony when Inditex listed in 2001. He has almost never accepted national honours, apart from a workers' medal in 2002. His colleagues said he resented O'Shea's book when it came out. At a surprise 80th birthday party in 2016, a video showed him tearful and backing away from the staff who had gathered to cheer him.
The only people I want to recognise me in the street are my family, friends and workmates.
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, in The Man from Zara, via CFI.co

blocks.text: Sometimes it went further. “Many times I think I would even like to change my appearance,” he told O'Shea, “so I could carry on with my usual life and nobody would talk about me.” People in A Coruña are used to seeing him out walking, ¡Hola! reports. In his own city, he seems to have found a version of that wish.
The rare moments he spoke

El País wrote in 2013 that he had never granted a single interview, and most reports repeat that. One of the best first-hand glimpses was an accident. Weeks before the 2001 listing, a Forbes reporter bumped into him in the staff canteen at headquarters. Forbes described a short, friendly man in slacks and an open-necked shirt who made small talk for a few minutes and then quickly disappeared. Fortune's request in 2013 was refused like all the others, and in 2026 ¡Hola! reported he was set on not telling his story.

The emotional moments reach us through O'Shea alone. Visiting his first Paris shop in 1990, he says, he could not get through the queue on the street and stood in a doorway crying. At a store opening in Manhattan, he shut himself in a bathroom and wept, thinking of his parents. For a man with no public face, it is a surprisingly tender public record.
How proud they would have been of their son who had, so to speak, discovered America, starting from a little town lost in the sticks of northern Spain!
blocks.who: Amancio Ortega, to Covadonga O'Shea, via Fortune

blocks.text: No ads, no accounts, no founder selfies

__He made the shops do the talking.__ Inditex is known for spending almost nothing on classic advertising, and relies on location and reputation instead. Manager magazin says he picked many early sites himself, driving through European city centres with his property team and stopping when he liked a building. Rent did not stop him. Top streets were his billboard.

There is no founder account either. His foundation says in writing that Ortega and Flora Pérez have no social media profiles and take no part in social networks. So treat anything online using his name as fake. In a time when young founders are told to build a personal brand first, he is a useful counter-example, with a warning attached in the next chapter.
Personal brand optional. Great product not optional.
How different countries see him

In Galicia he is a local hero: Fortune called him a small-town hero at heart. Across Spain the picture is split. The Merco reputation ranking put Inditex first among Spanish companies for years, and placed him fourth among business leaders in 2020.

During the pandemic, Galicia's regional president said he could not imagine medical supplies reaching Spain without the company's planes. Yet in 2021 Podemos politicians called Ortega a tax evader on social media. We found no court ruling or tax finding against him personally that supports the word, so it remains a political charge.

__Outside Spain, the brand is famous and the man is not.__ Fortune noted that among Zara's millions of shoppers, few had heard his name. Activists abroad judge the company by factories in places like Brazil and Turkey.
And in India

In the Indian business press we read, the man barely appears and the shop does all the work. Zara came through a joint venture with Tata's Trent, and the Economic Times says it is one of the most successful foreign fashion brands in the country, at first doubling sales about every two years. The paper describes the model as affordable, “copycat” versions of the latest fashions, made fast. Where Ortega himself shows up is in founder writing. Indian entrepreneur Alok Kejriwal read The Economist's 2016 profile and set out his own lessons from it, placing Ortega's hunger beside Dhirubhai Ambani's early years at a petrol pump.

__The Indian story is also a lesson in who holds the power.__ Inditex controls the product, sourcing and brand, and Trent says it treats the venture as a financial investment. Trent cut its stake from 49% to 20%. Meanwhile, Tata built its own fast-fashion chain, Zudio, to 963 stores by March 2026, against 22 for Zara, whose India revenue slipped 1.2% to ==₹2,749 crore== in FY26.
Trent kept a small stake and put its energy into its own brand.

This chapter is about the company he built and still mostly owns. We found no public statement from Ortega himself on any of these cases, and no report of any court finding him personally responsible. __His silence is itself part of the story.__ Each case below gives what was alleged, what the company said and how it ended, as far as public records show.
Brazil: the workshops in São Paulo

In 2011, Brazilian inspectors raided small workshops in São Paulo sewing clothes for Zara. They found 15 immigrants, mostly from Bolivia, working long hours in cramped, unsanitary conditions. Brazilian media reported that they earned the equivalent of 7 to 12 US cents a piece. Inspectors classed it as conditions analogous to slavery.

Inditex said a supplier had subcontracted the work without its knowledge, and that the supplier was paying compensation. In December 2011 it signed a deal with prosecutors, which press reports valued at US$1.8 million, against an original figure of US$10.

7 million. Zara Brasil also went to court to cancel the inspectors' findings and stay off Brazil's public “dirty list” of employers. In April 2014 a São Paulo labour court rejected that, with the judge finding it hard to believe Zara had such loose control over a workshop whose staff sewed only its clothes.

items.text: A labour ministry report cites problems at 67 factories. Inditex disputes it, calling it full of inconsistencies, and says it is preparing legal action.
New agreement with prosecutors widens Zara's legal duties. It pays R$5 million for breaching side clauses; prosecutors say no slave-like labour was found in that audit.
A São Paulo regional labour court holds Zara responsible for the 2011 case. Prosecutors say the judge called its claim of not knowing “convenient blindness”. Zara says it will appeal.

blocks.text: The money was small for a giant. The damage was to the story. A company famous for controlling every step argued in court that it had not known what happened in its own chain. __You cannot boast about controlling your supply chain and then plead ignorance when it fails.__
Very important for first-time founders! Own your whole chain, or don't claim it.
Turkey: the notes in the pockets

In November 2017, shoppers in Istanbul found tags hidden in Zara clothes. “I made the item you are going to buy, but I haven't been able to get my money,” they said. The factory, Bravo Tekstil, had shut overnight in 2016, and one worker told the BBC the boss had simply disappeared. About 140 to 155 workers said they were owed three months of wages and severance.

Inditex's answer was that it had paid the factory all it was due, but that the money never reached the workers. It set up a hardship fund with Next and Mango, reported at €210,000, while a union said that covered only a quarter of the losses. In 2018 the workers accepted partial payments. Clean Clothes Campaign, an activist group, says some of them got nothing. Inditex's Turkish sustainability manager had called it “an unjust suffering” but said the fault lay with the local firm.
Legally clean is not the same as morally finished.
Bangladesh: Rana Plaza

When the Rana Plaza building collapsed in April 2013, more than 1,100 garment workers died. Clean Clothes Campaign listed Inditex's Lefties among brands linked to the factories, through agents, before 2012. Sourcing Journal reported that Inditex did not source from there at the time.

Inditex was among the first to act afterwards. It backed the legally binding Bangladesh safety accord in May 2013, an agreement it signed as an original member, and was one of the first five donors to the victims' fund, giving ==$1.63 million==.
Taxes: legal, and still argued about

In December 2016, the Greens group in the European Parliament published a report saying Inditex had saved at least €585 million in tax from 2011 to 2014. It pointed to royalties paid to a Dutch unit, and to companies in Ireland and Switzerland. The report itself said these methods were legal. No court case came with it.

Inditex hit back the same day. It said the report rested on mistaken premises, that its tax rate was 22% to 24%, and that it had paid more than €4.4 billion in corporate tax worldwide from 2011 to 2015, half of it in Spain. The Greens' figures are their own estimate, and the company disputes them.
Legal does not mean finished. Public opinion runs a separate court.
Forced labour claims: complaints that have not led to a case

In April 2021, French campaign groups and a Uyghur woman filed a complaint accusing Inditex, Uniqlo, SMCP and Skechers of profiting from forced labour in Xinjiang. Prosecutors opened a probe, then closed it in 2023, saying they lacked jurisdiction. A second complaint was refused by a judge in 2024, and the Paris appeal court confirmed that in February 2025, though AFP reported a further complaint was coming. Inditex has always denied the claims and cites strict traceability checks. The latest report we found makes no finding of guilt.
Unresolved means unresolved. Be careful repeating this as proven fact.

In April 2024, the investigative group Earthsight linked cotton used in H&M and Zara clothes to land grabbing and illegal deforestation in Brazil's Cerrado. Inditex replied that such practices should never be allowed, and that according to its suppliers, the firms named did not buy directly from Brazilian producers. Earthsight says Inditex gave no evidence for that. __It shows how far a brand can sit from the problem and still be asked to answer for it.__
Products nobody should have approved

__Speed has a price in judgement.__ A company creating thousands of designs a year will sometimes ship one that should never have left the building. In several cases, a single complaint or a social media storm did what internal review had not.

items.text: A handbag from an Indian supplier carries swastikas. In Hindu tradition it is a sacred sign; a British customer saw a Nazi one. Zara pulls the range.
A striped children's shirt with a yellow star draws comparison to Holocaust camp uniforms. Zara withdraws it and apologises, citing western films.
“The Jacket” campaign, shot before the war, shows wrapped figures that critics liken to Gaza's dead. Zara pulls it and regrets the “misunderstanding”.
UK regulator bans two Zara images for making models look unhealthily thin. Zara says both models had medical certificates, and removes the images.

blocks.text: Indian readers: one symbol, two histories. Know what your product means elsewhere.

The most serious internal claim came in June 2015. Ian Miller, general counsel of Zara USA, sued for $40 million. He alleged he was harassed and fired for being Jewish, American and gay, and that senior executives were shielded by Ortega. These were allegations, not findings. His lawyers' website says the matter “was concluded in 2018” and gives no terms.
At home: the shop assistants' strike

__The company born from a shop assistant's insight ended up facing a strike by its own shop assistants, in its home province.__ On Black Friday 2022, shop staff across A Coruña province walked out, and most Inditex stores there closed. Union sources told El Salto that women in the shops earned about €1,080 for full-time work, against about €2,060 on a full-time warehouse contract. Business Insider España reported that inside Inditex, shop assistants were called “las niñas”, the girls.

It worked. In December 2022, after the staff threatened to strike again on the eve of Christmas Eve and on the first day of the sales, the union announced a deal worth €322 a month, rising to €382 within 22 months. The head of Zara's works committee put it at about 25%. The earlier national deal, signed by other unions, had been €180 phased in over three years.
He began as a shop assistant. Then his shop assistants had to strike.
The bad calls he made himself

The most personal failure was in September 2005. Ortega, a builder and a Galician savings bank tried to buy 22% of the power company Unión Fenosa from Santander. They lost it to the construction group ACS. Castellano later told El Mundo that the bid had a fatal flaw: buying that stake would have forced a much bigger takeover offer, and he said he was consulted only when it was too late.

That same day, his closest colleague resigned. La Voz de Galicia reported the partners had offered Castellano the chair of the power company, and that Ortega vetoed it. El País reported irreparable differences. Inditex said “personal reasons”. Castellano told El Mundo that neither man had taken it well, after seeing each other nearly every day for 31 years.
I simply refused to be part of a failure that had nothing to do with me.

blocks.text: There were product failures too. Uterqüe, Inditex's attempt at premium accessories launched in 2008, never quite broke into its segment, and all 81 shops closed in early 2022, with parts of its range folded into Massimo Dutti. The Spanish magazine Emprendedores called it the group's first big failure.

Then there is copying, the accusation that has followed Zara for decades. Asked about it, Ortega told O'Shea simply that “we all take inspiration from one another”. That is not a full answer to a designer who feels copied.
‘Everyone does it’ is never a real answer. Remember this one.
What not to copy

Do not copy the silence. It worked for his privacy, but it left workers, critics and shoppers with no founder to answer them when things went wrong. Do not stretch your chain so far that you cannot see who is sewing your clothes, then blame the last link.

And do not launch a big deal outside your circle of trust and tell your best colleague at the last minute. In 2012, Greenpeace pushed Zara to promise toxic-free production by 2020 after only nine days of public pressure. That is the positive lesson: __when the company listened, it could move as fast on doing right as on fashion.__
2 November 2026 was a payday. It was the date Inditex set for the second half of its dividend, ==€0.875 a share==. By our arithmetic, on his 59.3% stake that comes to about €1.
6 billion, for one day. It is half of a record €3.23 billion for the year. He is 90 years old, and he has reportedly not stopped going to work.
€1.6 billion in one day. He started with 2,500 pesetas.
What he still does

On paper, he has not run the company since July 2011. Pablo Isla took over as chair, and on 1 April 2022 Marta Ortega became non-executive chair, with Óscar García Maceiras as chief executive. __But he never fully left.__ He has sat on the board since 1985, the only director to do so for four decades, and was re-elected in 2023 for a term running to 2027.

The board's own records show how seriously he takes it. El Confidencial reported from company filings that he attended 97% of meetings from 2019 to 2023. His pay for this was just €100,000 last year, a rounding error beside the dividend. He also holds posts in companies of Pontegadea, his family investment group, many of them as chairman.

The Retail Gazette and ¡Hola! both report he still visits Arteixo. ¡Hola! says he keeps a table in an open space, eats with staff many days, and listens to young designers. ¡Hola! quotes his circle saying it is not about control and that “Marta is the boss”, but he likes seeing the machine run. In Galician, he likes to “enredar”: to tinker. This comes from friends, not from him, so read it as a friendly account.

blocks.text: The current bets

His dividends now go into a second empire. Forbes wrote in April 2026 that he has become the richest real estate owner in the world. He made 13 property purchases in 2025 alone, across 10 cities in 8 countries, spending more than $3 billion. One was the old Canada Post building in Vancouver, leased to Amazon, for about $850 million in cash, the largest office sale in Canadian history.

The pattern is shifting from buildings to the boring things that move goods. Pontegadea took 49% of British port operator PD Ports, and a year earlier it went into the car-park business with Q-Park. In August 2026 it closed a deal with Macquarie and UniSuper for Australian logistics firm Qube, valued at about A$11.
7 billion, and Pontegadea's share is 15%. It also holds stakes in energy grid and gas networks. __The boy who started in a shirt shop now owns the kind of assets that pay rent for decades.__
Notice: he never bought fame. He bought things that pay every month.
The bet that outlives him

The most visible near-term result is medical. Spain's first public proton therapy machine, in Santiago de Compostela, was due to be handed over at the end of October 2026, followed by final calibration. The centre hoped to treat patients late this year or early next, and a Spanish health ministry plan says the first patients come in early 2027. All 10 should be working between 2028 and 2029.

The foundation has told the public where the money goes next. It plans to spend ==€511 million== more through 2030, nearly all on social and health projects. Sick children in Spain may end up knowing the name better from a hospital than from a shop.
What he says he wants next

Nothing. That is the honest answer. His foundation says he holds no public conversations about business or charity, and we found no statement from him about his plans, his legacy or succession. What he wanted, he arranged long ago. He split ownership from management, moved the chair to his daughter while still alive to watch it, and kept most of the shares with the family.

So we can only read him by what he does each morning. In January 2026, the first Zara shop closed its doors, 50 years after it opened, while the group kept growing around the world. He is the longest-serving director on Spain's main stock index, and he has worked in clothes for more than 70 years. __He is still doing what he says he enjoys most: working.__
I go to the gym every morning. I like to chat, listen to people, meet new people, go for walks and, of course, work, which is what I enjoy most.

lessons.title: Stand where the customer stands.
lessons.text: As a teenage shop hand, Ortega had no say in what the store bought, so he watched what people actually wanted. That habit became a company. Spend your first months beside your customer, not behind a laptop.

lessons.title: Hire for what you cannot do.
lessons.text: He accepted that strategy, finance and logistics were not his strengths, and gave them to José María Castellano and later Pablo Isla. His limited English was handled the same way. Knowing your gaps is a skill, and it costs far less than hiding them.

lessons.title: Make yourself easy to reach.
lessons.text: At Zara Woman, staff told Fortune you did not need an appointment to ask Ortega a question. A founder with no door hears bad news early. Tear down whatever stands between you and your newest employee.

lessons.title: Build a system, not a secret.
lessons.text: Uniqlo's founder made beating Zara his stated goal, and Esprit's shares jumped 28% just for hiring an ex-Inditex logistics boss. Anyone can copy your product photo. Make the thing that delivers it the part that is hard to copy.

lessons.title: Never get comfortable.
lessons.text: “Complacency is the worst,” he told professors in 2007, when Inditex was already huge. He says you must turn an organisation upside down every day. If your last quarter feels great, that is the moment to look for what is breaking.

lessons.title: Take the lamp out of the window.
lessons.text: He once ordered a fancy lamp removed from a test shop because it looked too showy for Zara. Small details tell customers who you are. Be strict about the tiny things that don't fit your brand.

lessons.title: Delegate fully, then stay close.
lessons.text: He admits giving up the commercial side was hard, and that he used to have a view on everything. His rule became full trust, with people knowing they are not alone. Delegate, then stay close enough to help, not to hover.

lessons.title: Keep learning after school ends, and don't skip it.
lessons.text: He calls his work his university, but also says he regrets not studying more and not speaking English. Then he paid for over 5,500 teenagers to study abroad. Learn English now; it is the regret he names first.

lessons.title: Let the product do the shouting.
lessons.text: Zara grew with almost no classic advertising, using top streets as its billboard, while its founder stayed out of photos until 1999. You don't need a personal brand to win. You do need something people return for.

lessons.title: Take responsibility for your whole chain.
lessons.text: In Brazil, Zara argued it had not known about workshops making its clothes, and in 2017 a court called that convenient blindness. If your name is on the label, every worker behind it is your problem. Check before someone else does.

lessons.title: Legal is the floor, not the ceiling.
lessons.text: The Bravo Tekstil notes in 2017 showed Inditex could pay a factory in full and still see workers go unpaid under its brand. Tax planning that a report itself calls legal still became a public fight. Ask whether you could explain the decision to the person it hurts.

lessons.title: Remember who you used to be.
lessons.text: A company born from a shop assistant's insight faced a strike by shop assistants in its home province in 2022, and only then agreed a rise the union put at about 25%. Fix pay and respect before people need to walk out. Growth makes it easy to forget where you came from.

lessons.title: Never surprise your best partner.
lessons.text: In 2005, the failed Unión Fenosa bid ended a partnership of about 31 years, with Castellano saying he was asked in too late. Your closest colleague should hear about big moves first. One bad week can undo decades of trust.

lessons.title: Plan your exit while you can watch it.
lessons.text: He brought in Pablo Isla as chief executive in 2005 and handed him the chair in 2011, then watched an outsider run the company for years before his daughter became chair in 2022. Separating ownership from management let the business outgrow him. Start your own succession thinking long before you feel you need it.

lessons.title: Put your winnings into things that pay.
lessons.text: Since 2001 he has spent about $24 billion on 216 properties and sold only a handful, instead of buying fame. Save and invest early, even in small amounts, and let the income compound. Boring assets pay for bold giving, like the cancer machines his foundation funded.

factCheck.method: Four researchers wrote this book in parallel from company pages, results releases, press reports and extracts of Covadonga O'Shea's biography; a separate fact-checker then opened the sources directly on 3 November 2026 and rechecked the hook, numbers, dates, quotes, ventures, contact details and photo licences (through the Commons API), correcting what did not hold up and cutting what could not be confirmed. That check could not open The Times, The Telegraph, two Reuters stories, Better Retailing, SOMO's reports, Mind the Gap or Faro de Vigo, because they were blocked or paywalled, so claims resting only on them were re-sourced or removed, including every quote from The Times's 2003 article. Forbes's 2015–2017 and 2026 articles, The Economist's 2016 article and Bloomberg's profile also could not be opened normally, so they rest on the headlines listed on Forbes's profile page, reports summarising Forbes, passages quoted by Alok Kejriwal and a search-index copy of Bloomberg dated 11 October 2026. O'Shea's book itself was not available: it is cited through her publisher's press dossier, Cinco Días, Fortune and reviews, and quotes marked as translated, plus short Spanish phrases rendered in English, are our own translations; one set of machine-translated reading notes was used for paraphrase only.

disputed.claim: When the family moved to A Coruña
disputed.note: Fortune (2013) says the family moved when he was small; Le Petit Journal and El Cronista give 1944; Vozpópuli and El Español say he was about 12; Forbes (2001) says he came as a teenager in the early 1950s. The text uses 1944.

disputed.claim: His first job and the age he started
disputed.note: Fortune says he was barely a teenager when he became a shop hand at Gala. Gale's directory and Le Petit Journal say 13; El Español, ARA and CNBC say he left school at 14. In the publisher's extracts of O'Shea's book, Ortega says it is true he started work at 13. The text gives 13 or 14 and reports his own words.

disputed.claim: First public photograph
disputed.note: Fortune and El Debate agree no photo of him was published until 1999 (El Debate: in Inditex's first annual report). Other accounts describe his first public appearance in 2000, ahead of the 2001 stock-market listing. Both can be true; we use the 1999 photo.

disputed.claim: Has he ever given an interview?
disputed.note: El País (2013) and many others say he has never given one; Forbes (2001) records a few minutes of accidental small talk in the canteen, and O'Shea's book rests on long conversations. The writers also cited a 2003 Times article described as a meeting with him, but the fact-checker could not open it, so its quotes were removed from this book. We say he almost never gives interviews.

disputed.claim: Who founded Zara and Inditex
disputed.note: Forbes says he co-founded Inditex with his then-wife Rosalía Mera (died 2013) in 1975; Inditex's own history names Ortega as founder and dates Inditex itself to 1985, with the first Zara store in 1975. We say he opened the first Zara store with Rosalía Mera.

disputed.claim: Portrait photo
disputed.note: Wikimedia Commons has one image of Ortega (File:Amancio-ortega.300w.webp, 300×407 px) marked 'own work, CC BY-SA 4.0' by a one-time uploader. Its size and file name look like a resized image copied from a website, so we doubt the licence and did not use it. Portrait is left empty.

disputed.claim: Instagram @inditex
disputed.note: The Instagram handle @inditex is not verified, had six followers when checked and links to a Telegram channel. It is not an official Inditex account and is left out.

disputed.claim: How old he was when a shopkeeper refused his mother credit.
disputed.note: Fortune, citing his biographer, says 13. In the publisher's extracts of O'Shea's book, Ortega himself says 'apenas doce años', barely twelve. The text gives his words and notes Fortune's figure.

disputed.claim: His father's exact railway job.
disputed.note: El Cronista calls him head of the Busdongo station; Fortune, Vozpópuli and El Español just say railway worker; Diario de León says 'ferroviario de Renfe', though RENFE was only created in 1941. In the publisher's extracts of O'Shea's book, Ortega says he was a 'montador de enclavamientos' who watched over points and track. The text follows Ortega.

disputed.claim: His mother worked as a housemaid.
disputed.note: Fortune and Gale say housemaid; Vozpópuli calls her a housewife (ama de casa). El Español gives her name as Josefina, but Ortega's own account in O'Shea's book says Josefa, which the text uses.

disputed.claim: How long the family stayed in Busdongo.
disputed.note: Diario de León says a few weeks; Spanish Wikipedia (citing La Opinión A Coruña, which could not be opened) says about three months; El Cronista says he was still a baby. The text says 'a few weeks or months'.

disputed.claim: When he joined La Maja.
disputed.note: Vozpópuli says he started at La Maja as an errand boy at 14; other accounts (El Español, Fortune, Gale) put the Gala shirt shop first, and Spanish Wikipedia leads say he moved to La Maja at 17. The text puts Gala first and flags the conflict.

disputed.claim: He attended a Colegio del Sagrado Corazón.
disputed.note: Vozpópuli places this at about age 12 without naming the city clearly; Spanish Wikipedia places the Sagrado Corazón school in Tolosa. The text names the school but not the city.

disputed.claim: Wording of the O'Shea family quote.
disputed.note: El Cronista's article body gives 'nos educaron con valores' while its headline and caption say 'en valores'. The text uses the body wording. The quote is reported as coming from O'Shea's 2008 book; the book text itself was not available.

disputed.claim: Rosalía Mera 'started Inditex in 1963'.
disputed.note: The Local says so, but the Inditex holding company was created in 1985 (El Español). The text says she was part of the business from the start (GOA, 1963), not that she founded Inditex in 1963.

disputed.claim: What the name GOA stands for
disputed.note: Many profiles say GOA is Amancio Ortega Gaona's initials reversed; ARA (2025), drawing on Blanco and Salgado's book, says it came from the initials of Amancio and Antonio Ortega Gaona. The text gives both.

disputed.claim: Why 'Zorba' became 'Zara'
disputed.note: AP (via Boston Globe, 2013) and Il Post say a bar called Zorba was nearby and the sign's letters were reused; ARA (2025) says the name was already registered by another business. The text gives the bar version, attributed to the obituaries, and says elsewhere only that the name clashed.

disputed.claim: Share of Inditex sold in the 2001 IPO
disputed.note: BBC reported about 23%; the WSJ (cited via Wikipedia) about 26%; Forbes's preview said about a quarter. All agree Ortega's stake fell to about 60%. Text says 'part of it'.

disputed.claim: Zara's design-to-shop time around 2000
disputed.note: Company history says 10–15 days; Forbes 2001 says about three weeks from approving a design to delivery. Both are shown, attributed.

disputed.claim: When Lefties started
disputed.note: Wikipedia cites a Telegraph piece for 1993; Europe Real Estate (2025) says 1999. Text avoids a year.

disputed.claim: How long Often lasted
disputed.note: Company history dates its launch to 2003; FashionUnited (2006) says the experiment lasted 'almost two years'; idealista (2021) says three years. Text gives 2003–2006.

disputed.claim: Number of Uterqüe stores at closure
disputed.note: idealista: 82 stores at 31 July 2021; Emprendedores: 81 stores at the time of the closure announcement. Text says 'about 80'.

disputed.claim: Number of Russian stores closed in 2022
disputed.note: AP reported 502; Retail Gazette said 'more than 500'. Text says 'more than 500'.

disputed.claim: Ortega has never had an office or desk.
disputed.note: Fortune (2013) says he has never had an office, yet describes him at a desk at the end of the Zara Woman workspace. The Economist (2016, read through passages quoted by Alok Kejriwal) says no office, desk or desktop computer. Manager magazin says never an office. CNBC says he dispensed with an office and sits at a table. ¡Hola! (2026) says he has a work table in an open space. The title rests on the 'no office' claim; the text mentions the desk or table.

disputed.claim: Why José María Castellano left in 2005.
disputed.note: Inditex said 'personal reasons'. El País reported irreparable differences after the Unión Fenosa bid. La Voz de Galicia reported that Ortega vetoed a proposal to make Castellano chair of the power company. Cinco Días cited differences over management. Castellano told El Mundo it was about the deal alone, and that he had not negotiated it. The text gives each account with its source.

disputed.claim: How long Castellano worked with Ortega.
disputed.note: Castellano (El Mundo) and The Economist say 31 years, which would start about 1974. Cinco Días says about 20 years in senior posts, and other sections of this book date his hiring to 1984. Both may be true if he was involved earlier in a different role. We say 'about 31 years' when quoting him.

disputed.claim: When Ortega stepped down as chair.
disputed.note: Fortune, the Foundation and El Confidencial give 2011 (July, per Fortune). The Telegraph says 2012. The BBC calls him former chief executive. We use July 2011 for the chair.

disputed.claim: The value of the foundation's COVID-19 aid.
disputed.note: The foundation's own page says €47.5 million. El Confidencial reported €63 million in April 2020, when the programme was still under way. We did not state a single figure in the text.

disputed.claim: Date of the Zara swastika handbag.
disputed.note: Reuters and the BBC date it to September 2007. TIME (2015) says 2005. We use the contemporaneous 2007 reports. Inditex's spokesman said the design came from an Indian supplier and that the design it approved had no swastikas.

disputed.claim: Marta Ortega's first shop job.
disputed.note: El País (2012) says a Bershka store on Oxford Street in London. Vanity Fair (2025) says a Zara on King's Road. The text says only that she started on a London shop floor.

disputed.claim: The nature of the son's disability, and his birth year.
disputed.note: El País and others report cerebral palsy; one 2013 Spanish news report says Down syndrome. Sources also give different birth years (about 1971 to 1979). The text says only 'a severe disability', since the detail adds nothing.

disputed.claim: Whether Inditex sourced from Rana Plaza.
disputed.note: Sourcing Journal (2014) says Inditex did not source from those factories at the time. Clean Clothes Campaign (2013) lists Lefties among brands said to have used them through agents before 2012. A later paper by the Worker-driven Social Responsibility Network also lists Inditex among brands that had produced there. We report the two main accounts.

disputed.claim: Bravo Tekstil closure details.
disputed.note: The BBC and Inditex say July 2016, Clean Clothes Campaign says June 2016. Worker counts range from about 140 to 155. The text says 2016, and 'about 140 to 155'.

disputed.claim: First proton therapy treatment date.
disputed.note: The Xunta, El Correo Gallego and ABC say late 2026 or early 2027. Ministry plans reported by El Español say early 2027. Older reports gave earlier dates; the timetable has moved several times.

disputed.claim: Net worth figures.
disputed.note: Forbes showed $147.8bn (No. 12) on 2 Nov 2026. The latest Bloomberg copy we could read showed $126bn (No. 15), dated 11 Oct 2026. They count assets differently, and both move daily. Both are shown.

disputed.claim: How much money he started with
disputed.note: Ortega told O'Shea that he and his brother opened GOA's account with 2,500 pesetas (publisher's extracts); manager magazin also says 2,500. Forbes (2001) and the International Directory of Company Histories say 5,000 pesetas, 'about $25'. That dollar conversion looks low for the time, so we report it only as theirs. The text gives both sums.

disputed.claim: When Ortega and Rosalía Mera divorced
disputed.note: DPA, The Independent and El País say 1986. Il Post says they separated in 1986 and divorced officially in 1997. The text says they split in 1986.

disputed.claim: Property purchases in 2025
disputed.note: Spanish press citing filings counted at least 10 deals worth more than €1.65bn; another report in El Mundo says €3,000m. Forbes counted 13 worth over $3bn. The text gives both counts.

disputed.claim: Size of the 2011 Brazil settlement
disputed.note: The Jamaica Observer reported US$10.7m cut to US$1.8m. The fact-checker could not open SOMO's report, cited by the writers for R$20m and R$3.5m, so the text uses the press figures in dollars.

disputed.claim: Shop and warehouse pay in the 2022 strike
disputed.note: El Salto, citing union sources, gives about €1,080 for shops and €2,060 for warehouse jobs. The writers cited Reuters for €1,058 and €2,011, which the fact-checker could not open. The text uses El Salto's figures, attributed.

disputed.claim: YouTube channel @inditex
disputed.note: The channel exists but showed no content when checked, and Inditex's contact page does not list it, so it is left out.

disputed.claim: Zara's first products
disputed.note: ARA (2025), drawing on Blanco and Salgado's book, says the first things Mera and Renedo sewed were baskets of baby clothes, before the bathrobes that became GOA's first hit. Company histories start with the dressing gown. The text follows the dressing-gown story and labels it as the company-history version.
